$comment: DevOps Team Training Assessment, built from training/devops-training-assessment-prd.md and its question bank. Corrections and omissions, all deliberate. (1) ARITHMETIC: the PRD says 24 scored questions and a raw maximum of 120, which assumes every question is scored and can earn 5. Q01 (roles) and Q02 (learner count) are context questions the bank itself marks unscored, and Q03's best answer is worth 3, because the bank scores every real outcome at 3 and only 'not sure yet' at 0. So: 24 questions, 22 scored, raw maximum 21 x 5 + 3 = 108. A test asserts raw_max equals the sum of the best answer to every scored question, so the two can never drift. Numbering matches the source bank exactly. (2) TRACKS: the PRD names eight recommendation tracks; seven are categories here. 'FinOps and operational efficiency' has no category because no question evidences it - nothing in the bank asks about cloud cost or resource efficiency - and a finding nobody's answers can produce would be a guess wearing a recommendation's clothes. Its paragraph is not carried. The eighth category, outcomes_and_format (Q03, Q23, Q24), holds the outcome, measurement and format questions the PRD scores but assigns to no track; it has no PRD paragraph, so its finding body is new copy rather than a borrowed one. (3) GATES: the PRD's five critical-gate rules. Training ownership (Q20), learning enablement (Q21) and operational ownership (Q19) are mandatory findings on the 0-point answers; Q19's 'depends on individual experience' scores 1 and is left to ranking, where its deficit still counts. 'Advanced training without foundations' is a prerequisite gate rather than a finding: containers/platform and DevSecOps are held back from the primary slot while the foundations deficit is high. 'Several tools but no standard workflow' is narrowed: no question asks how many tools are in use, so the gate fires on the workflow half alone - Q16's 'one-off scripts owned by individuals' - and not on 'work is primarily manual', which is no workflow rather than an unstandardised one. No gate is omitted outright. (4) NAMING: the engine stores the delivery format under the payload key migration_direction, which store.js, the result screen and the DB column all read. The key is a historical name from the bank that introduced the feature; the value here is a training delivery format. (5) LEAD: the PRD's L02 offered email or WhatsApp; the site is email-only. L04 drops the PRD's last option, 'Book a DevOps team training strategy session', because it is the CTA rather than a goal. L04 is exposed twice in the payload: as desired_help, the shared lead column store.js writes, and as main_goal, the context key this bank names.

categories.label: Infrastructure as Code and cloud operations

prerequisite_gates.rationale: Platform training for a team without Linux, Git, and cloud fundamentals teaches the slides, not the platform. The pathway is staged: foundations first.
Secure pipeline controls assume a team that can operate a pipeline and an environment. Without the foundations, DevSecOps training has nothing to attach to.

mandatory_findings.rationale: PRD section 8: no identified training owner is a mandatory priority. A programme nobody is accountable for is a calendar entry, and the blockers it meets stay met.
PRD section 8: learners with no protected practice time is a mandatory priority. Training that competes with delivery work loses to delivery work every time.
PRD section 8: unclear production responsibilities are a mandatory priority. A team that cannot say who responds to an incident cannot be trained to respond to one until it can.

PRD section 8: several tools with no standard workflow is a mandatory priority. The questionnaire never counts the tools, so this fires on the workflow half alone - automation that lives in one-off scripts owned by individuals.

strategy_directions.$comment: PRD section 10. One suggested delivery format for the programme. A stated preference on Q24 always wins for its own format; the inferred rules only apply when Q24 is 'not sure', so a prospect is never told a different format from the one they asked for without a conversation. Among inferred rules the lowest priority wins: coaching where expertise is thin, train-the-trainer for a large population, project-based where the outcome is a working thing measured by deliverables, a workshop for a small capable team, and a cohort for everyone in the 5-50 range. The hold fires when neither the outcome nor the format is known.

sections.title: Team and business context
sections.focus: Who is learning, and what for
sections.body: Only the outcome question here is scored, and lightly. The roles and the learner count decide how everything after them should be read — a four-person startup team and a fifty-engineer bank can post the same score and need entirely different programmes.

sections.title: DevOps foundations
sections.focus: Linux, Git, and the cloud basics
sections.body: Every advanced DevOps topic stands on these three. A pipeline course delivered to a team that cannot resolve a merge conflict or read a DNS record produces people who can follow the slides and nothing else, which is why a weak score here reshapes the rest of the recommendation.

sections.title: CI/CD and release engineering
sections.focus: Build, test, deploy, and roll back
sections.body: The heart of it. These four questions ask not whether a pipeline exists but whether the team could build, maintain, and troubleshoot one — and whether it could get a bad release back out again. A pipeline one person understands is a dependency, not a capability.

sections.title: Infrastructure as Code and cloud operations
sections.focus: Provisioning, environments, and running the cloud
sections.body: Infrastructure the team cannot rebuild from code is infrastructure the team cannot safely change, and operations that depend on two people or an outside supplier are operations that stop when they do. This section asks how independently the team can provision and run its own environments.

sections.title: Containers, platform, and automation
sections.body: Three questions about the practices that let a small team support a lot of software. They matter most where several teams repeat the same platform work, and least where the foundations are still missing — which is why this track is held back until they are in place.

sections.title: Security, observability, and reliability
sections.focus: Security in delivery, seeing failure, and answering it
sections.body: Security checks that happen late, monitoring nobody acts on, and incident response that depends on who is in the office are three versions of the same gap: the team can ship, but cannot yet be trusted to run what it ships. This section asks whether it could learn to.

sections.title: Learning readiness and enablement
sections.body: This section predicts whether the training works, rather than what it should contain. A programme with no owner, no protected time, and no plan for adoption produces certificates and nothing else — and two of the three answers here can override the rest of the score.

sections.title: Outcomes, measurement, and delivery format
sections.focus: How success is measured, and what shape the programme takes
sections.body: Two questions that decide what the training is for and how it should be delivered. Success measured by attendance is success nobody can argue with and nobody can act on; the format question feeds the suggested delivery format directly.

devops_foundations.title: DevOps foundations
devops_foundations.body: Start with a practical DevOps foundation covering Linux, networking, Git, cloud concepts, environments, and the software-delivery lifecycle.
actions: Run a short skills check on Linux, networking, and Git with the actual team, so the foundation course starts where they are rather than where the syllabus assumes.
Put every contributor on one review-based Git workflow this month — protected main branch, pull requests, one named reviewer — and treat the first merge conflict as a lesson, not a crisis.
Give the team a sandbox cloud account with a budget cap and a weekly task, so cloud concepts are learned by building something small and deleting it again.

ci_cd_release_engineering.title: CI/CD and release engineering
ci_cd_release_engineering.body: Prioritise a hands-on CI/CD programme that builds a working pipeline for a representative application and includes testing, promotion, approvals, monitoring, and rollback.
actions: Choose one representative application and make building its pipeline the training project — the team leaves with something running, not a certificate.
Have the team, not the trainer, write the pipeline configuration into the repository, so the knowledge lives with the code rather than with whoever ran the workshop.
Rehearse a rollback on a normal working day as the final exercise, and record how long it took; that number is the before-and-after measure.

iac_cloud_operations.title: Infrastructure as Code and cloud operations
iac_cloud_operations.body: Train the team on Infrastructure as Code, cloud networking, identity, environment design, change review, and repeatable operations.
actions: Pick one environment the team can afford to break and have them rebuild it from code during the programme, with state stored somewhere safer than a laptop.
Move configuration and secrets into a managed secret store as a training exercise, so the team learns the pattern on its own values rather than a demo.
Rotate cloud operations tasks across the whole team for a month after training, so knowledge stops sitting in the one or two people it currently sits in.

containers_platform_engineering.title: Containers and platform engineering
containers_platform_engineering.body: Consider containerisation and platform-engineering training focused on reusable templates, deployment standards, self-service, and operational guardrails.
actions: Containerise one real service end to end — build, scan, deploy, troubleshoot — before anyone opens a Kubernetes slide.
Turn whatever the strongest team already does into a template the others start from, and make improving that template part of the training.
Replace the one-off scripts owned by individuals with a shared, documented automation repository, and review changes to it the way you review application code.

devsecops.title: DevSecOps
devsecops.body: Add a DevSecOps track covering secrets, identity, dependency and image scanning, Infrastructure as Code checks, vulnerability handling, and secure pipeline controls.
actions: Add dependency and container-image scanning to the pipeline the team builds in training, so security arrives as part of delivery rather than as a separate course.
Have the team take every secret out of source, chat, and shared documents during the programme, and put the managed store they move to under review.
Agree who owns a security finding, how severity is set, and how fast it must be fixed — before the first scan produces one.

observability_reliability.title: Observability and reliability
observability_reliability.body: Train the team to build actionable observability, define service-health indicators, respond to incidents, test recovery, and improve reliability.
actions: Build one dashboard per critical service during training that answers "is this healthy right now", and delete every alert nobody would act on.
Write down who leads an incident, who communicates, and how it escalates — then run a tabletop exercise on the last real outage to test it.
Restore a backup into a scratch environment as a training exercise and time it. Recovery that has never been rehearsed is a belief, not a capability.

team_enablement.title: Team enablement and operating model
team_enablement.body: Combine technical training with role definition, internal documentation, pairing, office hours, and a handover plan so capability remains after the programme.
actions: Name one accountable training owner with the authority to remove blockers, and put their name on the programme before the first session is booked.
Block the practice time in calendars now — sessions, labs, and application to real work — and treat it as delivery work, because it is.
Decide how the new skills become the standard: which projects they land in, who the internal champions are, and what you will measure in three months.

outcomes_and_format.title: Outcomes, measurement, and format
outcomes_and_format.body: Your primary gap is not a technical skill but the definition of the programme itself: what the training is for, how you will know it worked, and what shape it should take. Decide the outcome, the success measures, and the delivery format before choosing a syllabus — training without a defined outcome produces attendance, and attendance is not a capability.
actions: Write down the one outcome the training must produce — a pipeline, a rebuilt environment, a shorter recovery time — in a sentence the whole leadership team agrees with.
Choose two operational or delivery metrics to measure before and after the programme, so success is something you can show rather than something you feel.
Pick the delivery format on the evidence — learner count, how focused the gap is, what support the team needs afterwards — rather than on what is easiest to schedule.

continuous_improvement.title: Advanced enablement
continuous_improvement.body: No single track stands out as your primary gap, which at this level is the finding. The work now is platform engineering, reliability, optimisation, leadership, and continuous improvement — holding the capability the team has and making it the standard rather than the exception.
actions: Turn your strongest practices into reusable templates and guardrails, so the next team does not have to learn them the hard way.
Give senior engineers a deliberate teaching role — pairing, office hours, internal workshops — so capability spreads rather than concentrates.
Re-run this assessment in six months with a different person answering, and compare, rather than trusting the impression.

managed_enablement.title: Ongoing coaching or managed enablement may fit
managed_enablement.body: Based on your answers, ongoing coaching or managed enablement is likely to fit: it is recommended when the organisation has limited internal DevOps expertise, the team needs support after training, or there is a critical production platform or transformation programme. We deliver the programme, stay with the team while the skills are applied to real work, and transfer the capability rather than keeping it.

discovery_first.title: Do not choose a format yet
discovery_first.body: You are not sure what outcome you want from the training and not sure how it should be delivered, which is an honest place to start and the wrong place to choose a format from. A short discovery conversation settles both; choosing a format before it would mean designing the programme around a guess.

workshop.title: Workshop
workshop.body: A workshop is recommended when the team has fewer than 10 learners, the gap is focused, the organisation needs a short intervention, and the target outcome is awareness or a specific capability. It is the right size for one gap and the wrong size for a team that needs to change how it works.

cohort_programme.title: Cohort programme
cohort_programme.body: A cohort programme is recommended when the team has 5–25 learners, capability is uneven, the organisation wants structured practice and mentoring, and a multi-week implementation pathway is appropriate. It is the default here because most teams are uneven, and unevenness is what a cohort is built to close.

project_based_enablement.title: Project-based enablement
project_based_enablement.short: Build it on your own application
project_based_enablement.body: Project-based enablement is recommended when the customer needs a working CI/CD pipeline, IaC environment, or monitoring platform, the team learns best by applying skills to its own application, and the organisation wants measurable implementation outcomes. The programme ends with something running, which is also the evidence that it worked.

train_the_trainer.title: Train-the-trainer
train_the_trainer.body: Train-the-trainer is recommended when the organisation has a larger engineering population, wants internal champions, and the programme must scale across teams or locations. It multiplies the training rather than replacing it, and the champions need protected time as much as the learners do.

ongoing_coaching.title: Ongoing coaching or managed enablement
ongoing_coaching.short: Support that continues after the sessions
ongoing_coaching.body: Ongoing coaching or managed enablement is recommended when the organisation has limited internal DevOps expertise, the team needs support after training, or there is a critical production platform or transformation programme. Training gives a team the skills; coaching is what stops them evaporating in the first difficult week.
